[Knoepfler](https://www.ipscell.com) has published a paper blasting stem cell clinics and calling for more FDA oversight (something currently under state medical board jurisdiction). [This](http://www.cell.com/cell-stem-cell/references/S1934-5909(16)30157-6) is the new paper being talked about. You'll notice that it has only 9 references, 3 of which are the authors' prior work. That's a pretty big red flag... very few references 3 of which are yourself. VERY big red flag.

So let's look at this paper a bit to see what all this unproven unregulated magic is about--

"Businesses marketing putative stem cell interventions have proliferated across the U.S. This commercial activity generates a host of serious ethical, scientific, legal, regulatory, and policy concerns."

WHY?

"Perhaps the most obvious regulatory question is whether businesses advertising nonhomologous autologous, allogeneic, â€œinduced pluripotent,â€ or xenogeneic â€œstem cell therapiesâ€ are exposing their clients to noncompliant cell-based interventions."

As far as I am aware none of those are legal in the US to begin with. I have never personally seen them advertised. The only treatments I have seen offered in the US are from a patient's own fat or bone marrow or from amniotic tissue allografts (donor). So why does the FDA need to up regulation? They have rules against this already. Calling for more regulation would increase FDA funding and pharma profits by suppressing the industry... wonder who funds this guy. Also, a good amount of regulating these clinics is NOT under FDA jurisdiction because there is no interstate trade, the cells are not being expanded, and it is being performed by a physician in their own clinic on a patient who consents to the non-FDA regulated/approved treatment.

"While travel from the U.S. to international â€œstem cell clinicsâ€ continues, the rhetoric of â€œstem cell tourismâ€ often fails to acknowledge the hundreds of U.S. businesses engaged in direct-to-consumer advertising of stem cell interventions."

Nothing really wrong here. Businesses advertise, hospitals advertise, even the government advertises. Most advertising is directly to consumers. You know who does a lot of it really... DRUG COMPANIES!!! Gee whiz, they should just advertise via doctors by like giving them free stuff... oh snap, they already do that too!!!

"Figure 1 shows the geographic distribution of such businesses across the U.S. Many stem cell companies employ multiple physicians and advertise interventions available at numerous clinics.... Possible factors include a relationship between number of clinics and population density, regional variations in use of â€œalternativeâ€ medical interventions, aging population demographics, and regulatory orientation of state medical boards and consumer protection agencies."

Cool, so aside from still being pretty cost prohibitive, some form of stem cell treatment is becoming pretty widely available for people across the country. Nice map!

"Most of the businesses we identified market autologous cell-based interventions, with an estimated one in five advertising allogeneic stem cell interventions sourced from amniotic material (17%), placental tissue (3.4%), and umbilical cords (0.6%). Some clinics market both autologous and allogeneic stem cells."

Amnion... amniotic allografts are an FDA regulated under Good Tissue Practices. It is procured, along with "placental tissue and umbilical" from c-section births. It under goes rigorous examination- donor questionnaires, bioburden and sterility testing, in some cases (not technically required) mycoplasma testing. It is intended for homologous use only. Papers citing the effectiveness and safety of amniotic allografts can be found going back to the 80's (at least).

"One business promotes access to what it claims are induced pluripotent stem cells. This company did not indicate the purported source of induced pluripotent stem cells or address whether they are derived on a patient-by-patient basis for autologous therapy. Another business markets access to what it describes as â€œembryonic stem cellâ€ interventions. In addition, we identified two clinics that marketed â€œbovine amniotic cells,â€ a xenogeneic product, for use in humans. Approximately 3% of businesses marketed stem cell interventions without mentioning a particular type of stem cells."

Yeah... so there are 4 clinics in the US that probably aren't going to be open much longer. If you're worried about it, really, you could just report them since (from what I know) that's all no-no's.

"U.S. businesses promoting stem cell interventions claim to treat a wide range of diseases and injuries, as well as advertising stem cells for cosmetic applications, â€œanti-aging,â€ and other purposes (Figure 2B)."

Well ya know, they're just so darn versatile!

"Some clinics occupy relatively specialized marketplace niches. For example, many cosmetic surgery clinics advertise such procedures as â€œstem cell faceliftsâ€ and â€œstem cell breast augmentationâ€ as well as sexual enhancement procedures."

These are pretty new applications, as far as I have heard they are fairly successful. For the breast augmentation they don't actually augment anything, it is more for healing purposes as far as I know (prevent scar tissue formation).

"Orthopedic and sports medicine clinics often promote stem cell interventions for joints and soft tissue injuries."

Orthopedics only got one sentence... orthopedics is the bulk of this business. Guess they don't do anything that exciting with it though. :(

"Other clinics take a much broader approach and list stem cell interventions for 30 or more diseases and injuries."

Again, just so darn versatile.

"Such businesses commonly market treatments for neurological disorders and other degenerative conditions, spinal cord injuries, immunological conditions, cardiac diseases, pulmonary disorders, ophthalmological diseases and injuries, and urological diseases as well as cosmetic indications. Many of these marketing claims raise significant ethical issues given the lack of peer-reviewed evidence that advertised stem cell interventions are safe and efficacious for the treatment of particular diseases."

[Neurological Disorders](http://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v441/n7097/full/nature04960.html)

[Spinal Cord Injury](http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2678281/)

[Immune Disorder](http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2817019/)

[Cardiac Disease](https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Vincent_Segers/publication/5564282_Stem-cell_therapy_for_cardiac_disease/links/544e5a2d0cf2bca5ce90af2b.pdf)

Really... no peer-reviewed evidence at all!? Do you even own a computer!? Since [1978](http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC1818641/pdf/canmedaj01422-0061.pdf) there has been peer reviewed evidence that amniotic tissue can be used in wound healing applications. It's versatility and the use of mesenchymal (bone marrow and fat stem cells) cell has come a long way from there, but it is just false to say that there is NO PEER REVIEWED EVIDENCE this stuff is safe or works. There is a TON of it. He goes on about this more, but my argument sticks. There is ample evidence that it is safe and effective to treat or aid treatment of diseases and disorders with MSCs and amniotic products.

"Our investigation was in part motivated by ethical, scientific, and regulatory concerns related to the proliferation of U.S. businesses engaged in direct-to-consumer marketing of stem cell interventions."

No, your investigation was meant to stir up a media frenzy to try to increase your funder's interests and push down small bio-tech firms. You want to push federal regulation of people's own bodies and infringe on the jurisdiction of state medical boards.

"The REGROW Act is an example of the current push from some political quarters and even from some individual stem cell researchers for lowering safety and efficacy standards for adult stem cell-based interventions. However, we found that hundreds of U.S. businesses are already promoting stem cell interventions for an extraordinary range of clinical indications."

So the industry is willing to work to increase quality standards and increase access for people who need stem cell treatments. [The REGROW Act](https://www.kirk.senate.gov/?p=press_release&id=1691) appears that it would only really hurt big pharma profits. And again, we can't help it if MSCs have an extraordinary range of clinical indications, they're just that offing awesome.

"We are particularly concerned that we found many advertising claims related to ALS, Alzheimerâ€™s disease, Parkinsonâ€™s disease, and many other conditions for which there is no established scientific consensus that proven safe and efficacious stem cell treatments now exist."

[Absolutely (ALS)](http://www.fondazionevialliemauro.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/01/articolo-Stem-cell-treatment-in-Amyotrophic-Lateral-Sclerosis.pdf)

[No (Alzheimer's)](http://www.pnas.org/content/106/32/13594.full)

[Evidence (Parkinson's)](http://synapse.koreamed.org/search.php?where=aview&id=10.3988/jcn.2009.5.1.1&code=0145JCN&vmode=FULL)

And to conclude: "The best way to address ethical, legal, and scientific issues related to such businesses is to acknowledge their existence, examine and **evaluate their marketing claims**, and conduct public debates and policy discussions in the most evidence-based manner possible."

*Rage Face* Ok, so the ONE thing the FDA can pretty much regulate over everything is marketing claims. This regulation already occurs.
